answer: commit is a source control thing, so we shoudln't overload it. a ticket... no before we talk about that, this is something we've talked about before and if it's not in intentions it should be: a ticket carries it's workflow and status. it IS it's own manager. it asks a gate if it can transit the gate. if it's refused it has to get itself back to design for fixing. why is it that way?! because this format allows every workflow to be different. we add a new kind of thing we do, we build out the handlers for it, and then stamp it's workflow on it, and away it goes, NO OTHER EFFORT FROM US except to set the order things will be built in. so this harbor based analogy allows us to do that. if somebody doesn't have an available handler to ask, it throws a trouble ticket and then waits until we decide what to do. simple, yes?
